question: Thermal Properties of Matter: Define heat capacity and specific heat capacity.
gold_answer:
# Introduction

---

## Definition

Heat capacity and specific heat capacity describe how a material changes temperature when it absorbs or releases thermal energy.

Heat capacity is the total amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of an entire object by exactly $1 \text{ Degree Celsius}$ or Kelvin.

Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of exactly $1 \text{ kilogram}$ of a pure substance by $1 \text{ Degree Celsius}$ or Kelvin.

---

## Characteristics

* **Extensive vs. Intensive:** Heat capacity is an extensive property that scales with the size and mass of an object. Specific heat capacity is an intensive property inherent to the material itself, regardless of mass.

---

## Formula

The equations for thermal tracking are defined as:

$$\text{Heat Capacity } (C) = \frac{Q}{\Delta T}$$

$$\text{Specific Heat Capacity } (c) = \frac{Q}{m \Delta T}$$

Where:
* $Q$ represents the total heat energy transferred
* $\Delta T$ represents the resulting change in temperature
* $m$ represents the mass of the substance sample

---

## Summary

Heat capacity measures the thermal response of an entire object, whereas specific heat capacity standardizes this property per unit mass, providing an intensive material constant.

Heat Capacity & Specific Heat Capacity

Definition 01
Heat Capacity C
The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of a given body (as a whole) by 1°C (or 1 K), without any change in its state.

Definition 02
Specific Heat Capacity c
The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (or 1 K), without any change in its state.
🔑 It is a property of the material — independent of mass.

🔗 Relationship Between C and c
$$C = mc$$
Heat Capacity of a body = its mass × specific heat capacity of the material.
This means a larger mass of the same material has a higher heat capacity, but the same specific heat capacity.
📊 Comparison Table
| Property | Heat Capacity ($C$) | Specific Heat Capacity ($c$) | |---|---|---| | **Depends on mass?** | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | | **Depends on material?** | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | | **SI Unit** | J K⁻¹ | J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ | | **Extensive/Intensive** | Extensive | Intensive | | **Unique to an object?** | Yes (that body) | No (any sample) |
🌍 Real-World Applications
🌊 Water as a Coolant
Water has a very high specific heat capacity (~4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), making it ideal for cooling engines and regulating climate.
🍳 Cooking Vessels
Metals like copper and aluminium have low specific heat — they heat up quickly, making them efficient for cooking.
🌡️ Sea Breeze
Land heats faster than sea (lower specific heat), creating a temperature difference that drives coastal winds.
🏥 Hot Water Bags
Water stores large amounts of heat and releases it slowly — perfect for therapeutic heat packs.
📋 Specific Heat Capacities of Common Substances
| Substance | Specific Heat Capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) | |---|---| | **Water** | 4186 | | **Ice** | 2090 | | **Aluminium** | 900 | | **Iron** | 450 | | **Copper** | 385 | | **Gold** | 129 | | **Lead** | 128 |
⚠️ Important Notes
  • Specific heat capacity is measured at constant pressure ($c_p$) or constant volume ($c_v$) — for solids/liquids, the difference is negligible.
  • The formula $Q = mc\Delta T$ is valid only when there is no change of state.
  • $\Delta T$ in Kelvin equals $\Delta T$ in Celsius — only differences matter, not absolute values.
  • Water has the highest specific heat capacity among common liquids — a crucial fact for exams.
📝 Summary
✦ Heat Capacity — heat needed to warm a whole body by 1 K
✦ Unit: J K⁻¹
✦ Formula: C = Q / ΔT
✦ Specific Heat Capacity — heat needed per kg per K
✦ Unit: J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
✦ Formula: Q = mcΔT
🔗 Link: C = mc — the two quantities are connected through mass.
